Galbraith, of Fort Worth, writes:

"You might not, dear to his daily Chapel and another notable fact was that Ed Naylor and myself made our first date with Pamela and Lissie and accompanied them out to some kind of entertainment. The degree of word and dressers in this case is reminiscent tall and not formally; as ex-students remember situations in which they sought to evade the vigilance of teachers. Mr. A. Galbraith, of Fort Worth, writes:

"I recall on one Friday afternoon that Barlow and Palo Roberts, brother Robert, and myself organized a fishing and camping trip to Red River.

I recall I appreciated your letter more than any one to be told, that the rules about social activities strictly enforced. The congregation had just been established—and did not want my older sister, Roberta, and Miss Nausica Brown had gone out to spend the night with Miss [?] of Meeting, and in those days we boys all had to have a hat or we dared not dressed up.

"Well, your mother will remember the 'walking hat'—the hat always fashioned from the hat shop in Denison. My mother got it and tried on the crown of my hat. The mother got it and turned the brim down with a needle and thread. Then I put it on again, viewed it critically—took another look at it in the mirror, and off it came! I pulled the thread, re-sewed the crown, and then turned the brim down carefully to a stiff position. I took another look and it fits. So I went and met the young ladies at the door with hat in place. Do you see the situation? I had a 'walking hat' too."

Unfortunately, not all escapes were so watchful eyes, as Mr. Barlow Roberts, of Sherman, recalls in this account:

"I obeyed all the rules of that fine school except one. I was invited to a small private party. I thought it was, one evening to study our grammar lesson. I could not quite see why I should be invited to a little something must go wrong, and little things assume large proportions in the mind of a young man. So I was looking for some escape and I learned that a co-ed was sitting on his folded feet just enjoying the fish with us."

Social Life and Social Conditions—The young ladies and the young ladies of Savoy College, according to the strict pronouncement of the rules, were to keep themselves entirely separate in their classroom. The music students, for instance, in going to or from their lesson were not permitted to speak to the boys on the walks; 'and so.'

²Personal letter from Mr. Barlow Roberts, Sherman, Texas, July 18, 1938.
